title: Designing cases - state, questions, gold and thresholds

questions.prompt: What are the seven fields of a case in cases/routing.json?
options: id, group, class, state, questions, gold, thresholds
id, name, question, answer, score, notes, timestamp
id, group, class, state, questions, expected, limits
id, class, prompt, options, label, threshold, notes
questions.explain: Look at routing-001: it has id, group, class, state, questions, gold and thresholds - seven fields. Option 2 invents a name/score/timestamp structure that does not exist. Option 3 renames gold to 'expected' and thresholds to 'limits', which would break the runner: run_battery() reads case.get('gold') and case.get('class'), and the CLI reads case.get('thresholds'). Option 4 renames 'questions' to 'prompt' and 'options' - but the runner calls provider.decide(case['state'], case['questions']) and expects a dict of question objects.

questions.prompt: In cases/routing.json, what does the gold for the 'severity' question look like, and why?
options: A probability between 0 and 1, for example 'severity': 0.3
The level string itself, for example 'severity': 'Minor'
A number that is the INDEX of the level in the score question's criteria list - so 'severity': 1 means the second level, 'Minor'
A list of every acceptable level, for example 'severity': ['Minor', 'Major']
questions.explain: For a score question the gold is the level index, counted from zero: routing-002 has 'severity': 3, which is the fourth level in ["No impact", "Minor", "Major", "Critical"], i.e. Critical. collect_scored() reads the gold as a level index and compares it with abs(float(a['value']) - float(gold_value)) < 0.5, so a string gold would be coerced to 0.0 and the comparison would silently fail. A probability is not a label at all - it is what the model predicts, and metrics.collect_scored() would then compare the model's probability to your probability. A list of acceptable levels would break the comparison too.

questions.prompt: Why does every choice question in cases/routing.json include an 'other' option meaning 'none of the above - needs human triage'?
options: So that the model has a place to put its uncertainty, which raises its accuracy
So the options are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive - without it, a correct answer can be forced into a wrong bucket and you measure your taxonomy instead of the model
Because the provider API requires at least four options
Because the swap command needs a fourth provider
questions.explain: A choice question's criteria must be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. The 'other' option closes the set: if the ticket genuinely belongs to none of billing, technical or sales, there is a correct answer for it, instead of the model being forced to pick the least-wrong real team and being marked wrong for it. Without 'other', accuracy measures your taxonomy rather than the model - and a 'refuse' path that does not exist in the criteria is a policy hole. It does not raise accuracy (it may lower it, honestly). The provider API does not require four options. And the swap command compares two providers, not four options.

questions.prompt: What is the 'class' field on a case for, given that 'group' already buckets the cases?
options: It is the Python class used to build the case, for object-oriented dispatch
It lets you slice the results by difficulty and kind - clear-cut, borderline, spam - so you can see that a model is 100% on easy cases and 30% on hard ones
It decides which provider runs the case
It is a leftover field with no effect on the results
questions.explain: The classes in cases/routing.json are 'clear-cut', 'borderline' and 'spam' - a slice within the 'routing' group. run_report() groups scores by 'group', so the class is what lets you go finer: a model can look fine overall and be terrible on borderline cases, and a degenerate model that always answers the most common class will show up as a suspicious pattern in the clear-cut slice. It is a JSON string, not a Python class - there is no dispatch on it anywhere in the code. It does not select a provider (the CLI selects providers per run, not per case), and it is not inert: it is written into every JSONL record as 'case_class', so it is visible in the raw evidence.

questions.prompt: Connect this to the repo: why does a case carry several questions of different types instead of one?
options: So that the run takes longer and the latency numbers look realistic
Because the provider API charges per question, so more questions means a fairer cost comparison
Because 'questions' is a required field, so it cannot be empty

So a model cannot pass the battery by guessing one way - the case tests a yes/no judgement, a categorical choice and an ordered level, and the metrics can then compute accuracy, Brier and ECE from all of them
questions.explain: The three types probe different things and produce the (probability, outcome) pairs that metrics.collect_scored() needs: a noul question gives a calibrated probability against a boolean, a choice question gives a distribution against an option key, a score question gives a level against an index. Asking only one type lets a model game the battery - always answering 'billing' looks great on a billing-heavy set of choice questions. Latency is a side effect of work, not a design goal. Cost per question does matter for spend, but that is not why the battery is designed this way. And the field being required is a weaker reason: the point is coverage, and the metadata is there to make coverage possible.
